How political news reaches Americans, what they end up believing, and why the interventions built for platforms act on the wrong communication channels

The channels that cannot be counted are the ones that matter most.
Civic Health and Institutions Project (CHIP50), June 2022 – May 2026.

The ground this covers

Seven ways political news reaches people, sorted by what an outsider can observe about them rather than by technology. This is the landscape every estimate on this page was made across: who produces political news, how it is moderated, who passes it on, and where the available interventions stop.

The idea the map is a revision of

In 1944, studying how people made up their minds in a presidential campaign, Paul Lazarsfeld and his colleagues found something they had not gone looking for: mass media moved fewer votes than expected, and the people who did move were reached by other people. They called it the two-step flow — ideas travel from media to a smaller set of attentive people who interpret them, and from those people outward to everyone else. The second step happens in conversation, and it was always the harder one to see.

The obvious thing to say about the digital version is that algorithms removed the second step, delivering content straight from producer to person. That reading gets the theory wrong. Lazarsfeld and Katz never defined an opinion leader by closeness of tie; they defined one by function — someone who follows media more closely than most and interprets it for others, positioned within a group rather than above it. A podcaster, a newsletter writer or an influencer occupies exactly that slot, and a recommender does not replace step two so much as decide which step-two node you meet.

What has changed is the direction. The classic account is vertical: media at the top, opinion leaders below, the public below that. Hunt and Gruszczynski call what replaced it a “horizontal” two-step flow, in which influence moves sideways within peer strata in decentralised environments rather than descending from elites.

That is what the right-hand side of the map is. Read it from the middle outward: the reader receives, and then passes on — into group chats, into messages, into conversation. The classic second step ran through people whose influence could at least be described. This one runs through channels where the content and the audience cannot be counted at all, which is exactly where every instrument in the bottom band stops. The measurement problem and the theory are the same problem: the step that does the work is the step nobody can see.

Lazarsfeld, Berelson & Gaudet (1944); Katz & Lazarsfeld (1955); Hunt & Gruszczynski (2024). Full entries in the bibliography.

In brief. Almost everything known about political misinformation comes from the handful of channels an outside analyst can count, and every major intervention — deplatforming, downranking, labels, fact-checks, the DSA's duties — attaches to exactly those channels. Across fifteen waves of a national survey we map American political news use onto seven regimes defined not by technology but by what can be observed about them, and estimate what each one predicts across 31 beliefs and questions about institutional trust. The regimes do predict belief, and not in the order platform governance assumes: on election denial, podcasts and private messaging run ahead of the large platforms that are the near-exclusive object of regulation. More than that, the regimes are not one phenomenon with different strengths. Giving each the same three candidate explanations — how common a position is overall, how much it belongs to the answerer's own side, and which side of politics it sits on — separates them into distinct kinds: podcasts track sheer rarity, partisan broadcast and the big feeds track the distance between the parties, mainstream news and word of mouth pull in opposite ideological directions, and private messaging alone tracks how out of step a position is with the user's own side, carrying no ideological direction at all. That last pattern holds on trust in the police and the military as firmly as on conspiracy claims, survives with about 45% of its strength among people who report no party whatsoever, and is therefore not a story about misinformation travelling — it is a story about who occupies the channels nobody can audit. The theoretical cost is specific: a diffusion account, which predicts that what matters is how far a claim has spread, is the wrong model for private channels and the right one for podcasts, and the governance instruments, built without exception on the channels that can be counted, reach neither.

Unfamiliar words — regime, odds ratio, adverse, base rate — are defined in plain language in the glossary near the end.

Start here: three ways a belief can be unusual

Think about where politics actually reaches you. A group chat with old friends. A podcast on the drive. Your brother-in-law at dinner. The feed. The evening news. It is tempting to sort those by how trustworthy they are — but that is not what separates them in this data. What separates them is which kind of unusual a belief has to be before a source goes with holding it.

There are three different ways a belief can be unusual, and they come apart. Almost nobody thinks wind turbines cause cancer — that belief is rare everywhere. Trusting Donald Trump is not rare at all, but it is lopsided: common on one side of politics, rare on the other. And a belief that is your own side's is by definition the other side's unusual one. Those are three separate measurements, and in this data they barely overlap.

Before any of it: nothing on this page shows a source changing anyone's mind. People choose where they get their news, and the choosing runs on the same things the beliefs do. Every result below is “the people who use this are the people who…” and never “using this makes you…”. The full version of that warning is at the end.
